passage:
28 March. An agent phoned Gurpreet at closing time: "Sign today and you save tax, only this week." The plan cost 40,000 a year. Gurpreet signed on the phone, tired and relieved to have it done.
June. Hafsa, a colleague, asked what the plan covered. Gurpreet had never read the paper. Together they went through it. If something happened, the payout would be only 4,00,000. Gurpreet went quiet: ten years of premiums for that.
The next March. When the agent phoned again, Gurpreet said, "Send me the papers, I'll read them and call you." Hafsa sat beside Gurpreet with a highlighter, and the pages came out marked with questions, not signatures.

qa.q: How much did the plan cost each year?
What was Gurpreet feeling in June when reading the paper with Hafsa?
qa.a: Gurpreet was dismayed and felt foolish, shown by going quiet on seeing how little the payout was for ten years of premiums.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet try before buying anything late in the next March?
qa.a: Gurpreet could start comparing plans early in the year and ask a registered adviser what protection each one gives.

qa.q: How might Hafsa have seen Gurpreet's rushed purchase?
qa.a: Hafsa probably saw a tired colleague pushed by a deadline, not careless, and so offered to read the paper together.

grounding: The passage shows a person buying a low-cover plan under an agent's late-March push for tax benefits, then finding it gives little protection for the premium.

subtopic: Building insurance and an emergency fund
subtype: Approach: buying a policy only for tax saving [Pitfall]
passage: Uma, before you sign anything this March, sit with your Abhinav Mama for five minutes. The year I turned twenty-five, it was the last week of March and my office wanted tax proofs by Friday. An agent from our colony came home with a glossy folder. 'Sir, save tax and get returns also,' he said. I signed that evening without reading past page two. A premium every year for fifteen years. Three years later my father was admitted for his heart, and I opened that folder with shaking hands. The cover was so small it would not have paid for one week in the ward. I had been paying for a tax receipt, not for protection. After that, I asked an adviser who sold nothing to explain what I actually needed. So tell me, what are you buying, and why?

qa.q: When did Abhinav sign the policy?
qa.a: Abhinav signed that evening, in the last week of March, without reading past page two.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he opened the folder three years later?
qa.a: He felt frightened and foolish: his father was in hospital, and the cover turned out too small to pay for even one week in the ward.

qa.q: At that Friday deadline, what other choice could Abhinav have made?
qa.a: He could have asked for time to read the whole document, or checked with an adviser who sold nothing, instead of letting a tax deadline choose the policy.

qa.q: What would have changed for Abhinav's father if the policy had been bought for protection rather than tax?
qa.a: When his father was admitted, the family could have leaned on real cover for the ward bills instead of finding it would not last a week.

grounding: It shows a young man buying a low-cover savings plan in late March for the tax benefit on an agent's pitch, then finding it offers almost no protection.

subtopic: Building insurance and an emergency fund

passage:
March 31, 11.20 p.m., and the power was out across Saurabh's lane. His office portal would lock tax declarations at midnight. On his phone's last twenty percent of battery, an agent who had called all week kept repeating, 'Just pay tonight, sir, you'll get the deduction, and money comes back after twelve years.' Saurabh paid the first premium by torchlight at 11.52 and slept feeling clever.
In June his colleague Yamini was comparing policies over lunch. She showed him her plain term cover: a large payout to her family if she died, for a small yearly sum. Saurabh opened his own papers. For nearly four times her premium, his family would get a sum smaller than two years of his salary.
'So I bought a receipt,' he said quietly, pushing his plate away.

qa.q: At what time did Saurabh pay the first premium?
qa.a: Saurabh paid the first premium by torchlight at 11.52, just before the portal locked at midnight.

qa.q: What does Saurabh pushing his plate away suggest he felt in June?
qa.a: He felt deflated and embarrassed, because the policy he had felt clever about gives his family very little protection for what he pays.

qa.q: What else could Saurabh have done with the midnight deadline pressing?
qa.a: He could have let that one deduction go, and taken the policy question to a qualified adviser without a sales target once the lights were back.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Saurabh's purchase after they compared papers?
qa.a: Yamini may feel sympathy and some awkwardness, since her simple comparison showed that his bigger premium buys much less cover.

grounding: It shows a last-minute, agent-pushed tax-saving plan that later turns out to offer little protection for its cost.
